title: Encoding a bosonic mode into qubits for simulating boson-matter interactions
authors: Maarten Stroeks, Jelena Mackeprang, Yaroslav Herasymenko, Barbara Terhal
abstract: We explore the space-time cost of encoding of a bosonic mode into a set of qubits via various encodings, and their resilience to noise. In particular, we compare the performance of the unary Fock state encoding, an unexplored encoding of Fock states into Dicke states (``Dicke'' encoding), and the binary quadrature encoding. We do so by considering a displacement as well as a simulation of a Dicke model, coupling a bosonic mode to a set of atoms represented as qubits. Using classical simulations, we assess the accuracy and optimized space-time costs in terms of number of qubits, circuit depth and CNOT count of a quantum simulation of the time dynamics using these encodings. Although our study is far from comprehensive, we find that the binary quadrature encoding is overall most favorable in terms of being very space-efficient and relatively time-efficient due to the use of the quantum Fourier transform. Our novel Dicke encoding leads to very shallow circuits, but pays in terms of using many more qubits. We probe the use of an H2-2 Quantinuum trapped-ion qubit device (56 qubits) for displacement and Dicke model simulation in the low boson-number regime, where we find that noise leads to visible deviations from ideal circuit dynamics.
summary: This paper compares several methods for encoding a bosonic field into qubits to simulate boson-matter interactions. By analyzing space-time costs and noise resilience, the authors determine that the binary quadrature encoding is generally superior. The findings provide critical guidelines for mapping continuous quantum physics onto near-term quantum hardware architectures.
main_problem: The paper investigates the trade-offs in encoding a continuous bosonic mode into a discrete qubit system to simulate complex boson-matter interactions.
main_result: The binary quadrature encoding is found to be the most favorable approach, offering a good balance between space efficiency and time efficiency, although the Dicke encoding yields shallower circuits at the cost of many qubits.
method: The authors use classical simulations to compare various encoding schemes (Unary, Dicke, Binary Quadrature) by analyzing the space-time cost (qubits, circuit depth, CNOT count) and noise resilience for implementing key operations like displacement and Hamiltonian evolution.
model_or_system: The system involves simulating interactions between a bosonic mode (infinite-dimensional Hilbert space) and a set of qubits representing matter degrees of freedom. The core challenge is mapping the bosonic operators ($\hat{a}, \hat{a}^\dagger$) onto qubit operators ($\hat{x}_E, \hat{p}_E$).
key_observables: Encoding error (infidelity), circuit depth, CNOT count, and Trotterization error ($\epsilon_T$).
important_parameters: Boson number ($m$), number of qubits ($N_b$), displacement parameter ($\alpha$), and simulation time ($t$).
main_assumptions: The study relies on classical simulations for cost assessment, and the analysis of the commutator norm for the binary quadrature encoding is noted as potentially overly pessimistic.
figures_summary: Figures compare encoding error vs. $N_b$ for different encodings, and show circuit cost metrics (CNOT count, depth) for implementing time evolution under the Dicke Hamiltonian.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares multiple encoding methods (Unary, Dicke, Binary Quadrature) by analyzing the cost of implementing fundamental operations like displacement and Hamiltonian evolution, culminating in a comparison of error scaling and circuit resources.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the crucial resource overhead associated with quantum simulation, providing quantitative metrics to guide the choice of encoding scheme for implementing continuous variable physics on discrete qubit hardware.
